newsitem.title: USA: Blood, fingernails in O.J. Simpson testimony.
newsitem.headline: Blood, fingernails in O.J. Simpson testimony.

text.p: O.J. Simpson faced legal battles on two fronts on Tuesday -- in family court seeking full custody of his two children and in civil court defending himself against a wrongful-death lawsuit.

The former football star was absent from a Santa Monica courtroom where his lead attorney grilled a plaintiffs' witness in the civil case brought by the families of two murder victims, his slain ex-wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, and her friend, Ronald Goldman.

Instead, Simpson, who was acquitted in October 1995 of the murders, was 50 miles (80 km) south in an Orange County courtroom for the first day of trial in a battle against the parents of his ex-wife for custody of his daughter Sydney, 11, and son Justin, 8.

Louis and Juditha Brown have had temporary guardianship of their grandchildren since Simpson's arrest in June 1994, and they now want permanent custody. Simpson wants to regain sole custody. A judge will decide if they should live with their father or continue living with the Browns.

Meanwhile, in the civil case in Santa Monica, the trial took on a dramatic tone on Tuesday as Simpson attorney Robert Baker clashed with forensic pathologist Werner Spitz, an expert witness for the plaintiffs, during cross-examination.
At one point Baker tried to argue that scratches and cuts on Simpson's hand could not have been made by Goldman during his fatal struggle with a knife-wielding assailant.

Asked if he had concluded that Goldman's fingernails could not have caused "gouge" wounds to Simpson, Spitz replied "No, Mr. Goldman had short fingernails. I do too." He explained that even short nails could cause such injury.
At this point, Baker approached Spitz, holding out his forearm: "Gouge me!" he said.
"Do you want me to scoop tissue out?" asked Spitz in his heavy German accent.
Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki then interjected, setting off laughter in the court when he said: "Mr Baker, I'm not going to have any gouging of flesh."

Spitz, a retired county medical examiner in Michigan, then rolled up his own shirtsleeve to demonstrate. "When you are fighting for your life and dig in deep without concern if you are hurting, you pull back the fingernail and it becomes longer," said Spitz.

Asked specifically by Baker if Goldman could have caused the cuts on Simpson's hand, Spitz replied: "I am not able to look at fingernail marks and say who made them. I can say Mr Goldman could have made them."
He acknowledged no analysis had ever been made of Goldman's fingernails. Of Nicole Brown Simpson's nails, he said: I understand she had fake fingernails. They were glued on."
He said that there was a substance that could have been blood under her fingernails.
During cross-examination, Baker tried to get him to change his previous testimony that Nicole Brown Simpson died in about 15 seconds and that Goldman was left for dead after about one minute.
But the combative, white-haired pathologist stood his ground, often earning Baker's ire.
Goldman's father, Fred, and sister, Kim, bowed their heads and refused to watch as bloody crime scene photographs were shown to the jury. Simpson's elderly mother, Eunice, was also in court.
